P0: The monitor reads only public sources that need no account: esports and games news, the official League of Legends esports feed, OpenDota (Dota 2 data), Steam, deal sites, status pages and earthquake data. Each source is on a register with its fetch interval and a terms note. Five saved views show what each kind of user needs first. Still open: a careful licence check of every source.
P1: Every headline gets tags for the game, the kind of event (for example a roster change, a result, a deal or a ban) and the places it names. News sites that cover more than games must mention a gaming word, or the item is dropped. Unit tests check the rules. Still open: a measurement on a sample that a person labels by hand.
P2: A world map with four layers and 17 tiles that you can minimise or maximise. Each tile has a 'why this matters' note and a plain message when it has no data. Updates are pushed to the open page at once. A scripted browser walk checks every view at desktop width and at phone width.
P3: Steam player counts are stored every 5 minutes, with an estimate for the next hour. The estimate is shown only when it beats the simple guess 'the same as now' on past data. The database that changes often is stored outside the OneDrive-synced vault.
P4: GDELT, a global news index, blocks clients that ask too often, so the server waits longer after each refusal. PandaScore matches for all games, and a Claude-written brief with sources, are built and tested with sample data. They turn on with a key and need a real run to count as done. Liquipedia waits for the operator's approval of a contact email.
P5: The server runs in its own window. The project is on the trackdoc hub. Starting it at logon waits for the operator's approval.
